::: {.why}
There is a closed-form prediction for the spectrum of a pure-noise correlation matrix, and comparing your real one against it separates structure from sampling with no tuning parameter.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the Marchenko-Pastur edges in terms of the asset-to-observation ratio, and evaluate them for your own matrix.
- Report how many of your eigenvalues lie outside the predicted noise band, and what they correspond to.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the Laloux, Cizeau, Bouchaud and Potters noise dressing paper. It is short and it is the original statement of this comparison on financial data.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Overlay the theory on your data: plot the empirical eigenvalue density of your correlation matrix with the Marchenko-Pastur density drawn on top, with the edges computed from your own N and T. Count the eigenvalues above the upper edge and identify what the top two eigenvectors are loading on.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write down the interpretation: the largest eigenvalue is the market, the next few are usually sectors or styles, and everything inside the bulk is indistinguishable from noise at your sample length.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Laloux, Cizeau, Bouchaud & Potters (1998) — Noise Dressing of Financial Correlation Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9810255) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Bouchaud & Potters — Financial Applications of Random Matrix Theory (review)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.1205) [paper]{.res-kind}
